title: Keyboard Manager shortcuts cannot override Windows shortcuts
summary: Keyboard Manager remaps Win+Left and Win+Right to Home and End in the report, but Windows snap shortcuts still win. The exact failing remap stage is not established by the public evidence.

status.label: Low-confidence design - needs confirmation
status.detail: Trace the Win-arrow OS-level remap path and capture a diagnostic before selecting a root-cause fix.

next_action: Request targeted reproduction evidence; approve only the investigation plan, not an asserted root cause.

fix_assessment.rationale: The code has a plausible OS-level shortcut path to investigate, but no public trace proves whether registration, modifier state, or injection is failing.

judgment.rationale: The issue gives a sufficient A/B reproduction, while the source identifies the relevant Keyboard Manager OS-level shortcut handler and test seams. It does not justify claiming a specific failure mechanism yet.
evidence: Observed: the reporter maps Win+Left to Home and Win+Right to End, but Windows snaps the active window left/right.
Observed: the reporter is on Windows 11 26200.9168 and supplied no diagnostic ZIP.
Observed: Keyboard Manager handles WM_KEYDOWN and WM_SYSKEYDOWN in KeyboardEventHandlers and has dedicated OS-level shortcut tests.
Observed: Helpers treats VK_LEFT, VK_RIGHT, VK_HOME, and VK_END as extended/numpad-sensitive keys.
Inferred: the failure could be in shortcut matching, suppression ordering, or target injection; current evidence does not distinguish them.
judgment.recommended_action: Request a fresh diagnostic plus exact remap type and foreground elevation, while preserving a low-confidence code investigation plan.

issue_context.summary: Win-arrow remaps do not suppress Windows snapping and do not produce the configured Home/End target.
known_information: The issue is open and labeled Issue-Bug.
The expected target is Home/End and the actual behavior is Windows snap.
No diagnostic archive or follow-up discussion is present.
inferences: The remap may not be reaching the OS-level shortcut handler, or the original Win-arrow event may not be suppressed.
The arrow keys' extended-key handling is a plausible area but is not proven.
issue_context.analysis: Because Windows snap is observed, the original shortcut reaches the shell or foreground system. The source's OS-level remap path should be traced from KeyboardManager::HandleKeyboardHookEvent through shortcut matching and injected target events. A diagnostic is needed before converting that trace into a root-cause claim.

Read KeyboardEventHandlers.cpp and relevant helper/test code in the current checkout.

proposed_fixes.title: Trace and harden Win-arrow OS-level shortcut suppression
proposed_fixes.root_cause: Unproven. A plausible failure is that the OS-level shortcut handler does not match or suppress Win+Left/Right before Windows processes the shell shortcut, or injects Home/End with incorrect extended-key state.
plan: Trace KeyboardManager::HandleKeyboardHookEvent into HandleOSLevelShortcutRemapEvent and Shortcut modifier/action matching.
Compare the low-level event flags and encoded virtual keys for Win+Left/Right with existing extended-key handling for Home/End.
Add deterministic tests for matching, suppression, and injected target events for both arrows.
Use the requested diagnostic and a local trace to select the smallest fix; do not change shell behavior based on the issue title alone.
verification: With the exact remaps configured, Win+Left and Win+Right must no longer snap the active window and must produce Home and End respectively.
Normal arrow navigation and unrelated Win shortcuts must remain unchanged.

confidence.rationale: The handler and key families are confirmed, but the public report has no diagnostic or trace proving which branch fails.

design.root_cause: Not established. The strongest supported hypothesis is an OS-level Keyboard Manager shortcut path failure involving matching/suppression or extended-key injection, but the current evidence cannot distinguish those mechanisms.
evidence: src/modules/keyboardmanager/KeyboardManagerEngineLibrary/KeyboardEventHandlers.cpp contains OS-level shortcut handling for WM_KEYDOWN and WM_SYSKEYDOWN.
src/modules/keyboardmanager/common/Helpers.cpp explicitly handles arrow, Home, and End virtual keys as extended/numpad-sensitive keys.
The issue's observed Windows snap proves the original Win-arrow action is not being fully replaced.

Build Keyboard Manager engine tests using the repository-supported command.

risks: Keyboard Manager low-level changes affect all remaps and can strand modifiers or alter shell shortcuts.
An unproven fix to extended-key encoding could regress numpad behavior.
The reporter's preview/stable versions and OS build may differ from the local checkout.
alternatives: Change the mappings to another trigger. Rejected because it avoids rather than fixes the reported override failure.
Disable Windows snap. Rejected because it changes unrelated system behavior.
Claim a definite extended-key bug now. Rejected because no trace establishes that root cause.

notes: The plan intentionally remains red-confidence and makes the missing trace an explicit gate before implementation.

comment.body: Thanks for the concrete Win+Left/Right remap example. The current source shows several possible failure points (shortcut matching, original-key suppression, and extended-key injection), but the public report does not identify which one fails. Please reproduce both mappings, then add a comment containing `/bugreport`; also state whether each mapping is single-key or shortcut-to-shortcut and whether the foreground app is elevated. This will let us choose a targeted fix without guessing.
